title: IF GOD OPPOSES POLYGAMY, WHY DID HE COMMAND MEN TO PROVIDE FOR MULTIPLE WIVES? THE DISTURBING TRUTH BEHIND EXODUS 21:10
paragraphs: IF GOD OPPOSES POLYGAMY, WHY DID HE COMMAND MEN TO PROVIDE FOR MULTIPLE WIVES? THE DISTURBING TRUTH BEHIND EXODUS 21:10

One verse seems to contradict everything Christians believe about marriage. But when you discover who God was protecting, what the Hebrew actually says, and why Jesus pointed back to the beginning, you may never read the Old Testament—or understand God's heart toward wounded people—the same way again.
There is a question that has troubled Christians, emboldened skeptics, and left more than a few Bible readers staring at the page in uncomfortable silence.
If God's design for marriage is one man and one woman, why does His own Law tell a man what to do when he takes another wife?
Not merely acknowledge the possibility.
Not simply describe something that happened.
But actually give instructions about it.
Exodus 21:10 says:
“If he take him another wife; her food, her raiment, and her duty of marriage, shall he not diminish.” — Exodus 21:10, KJV
Read that again.

God is speaking through Moses. Israel has just been delivered from Egypt. The covenant law is being established. And there, among the commandments governing the lives of God's people, is a regulation concerning a man who takes another wife.
You can almost hear the objection.
“Wait. I thought God was against polygamy.”
And then comes the question that makes some believers nervous:
“Was God contradicting Himself?”
Perhaps you have wondered about it privately but were afraid to ask.
Perhaps someone used this verse to challenge your faith, and you didn't know how to answer.
Or perhaps you have watched people use the Bible to justify something that deeply wounded another human being, and you have wondered whether God was really on the side of the person who suffered.
Stay with me.
Because the answer is not found by pretending the verse doesn't exist.

It is found by reading the verse carefully, listening to the Hebrew, understanding the world in which it was spoken, and allowing Jesus Christ Himself to show us the difference between what God permitted in a fallen society and what He intended from the beginning.
And beneath this difficult question lies something deeply personal.
Something about the God who sees people others have learned to overlook.
Something about the difference between being legally protected and being genuinely loved.
Something about the terrible things human beings can normalize—and the extraordinary grace of a Savior who refuses to leave us where sin has taken us.
The first thing we must understand is that Exodus 21:10 does not appear in a chapter celebrating marriage.
It appears in a chapter dealing with servitude, vulnerability, and the responsibilities of those who possess power over others.
The immediate context is Exodus 21:7–11, a law concerning a daughter sold into servitude by her father, within an ancient social system profoundly different from ours.
That reality should disturb us.
We should not sanitize the vulnerability of the woman in this passage or pretend the arrangement reflects the freedom, dignity, and mutuality we should desire for women today.

In this particular legal situation, the woman could be designated for marriage within the household. The passage addresses what must happen if the arrangement is not fulfilled as expected, if she is assigned to the master's son, or if another wife is taken.
Then comes verse 10.
In Hebrew, the central command reads:
אִם־אַחֶרֶת יִקַּח־לוֹ שְׁאֵרָהּ כְּסוּתָהּ וְעֹנָתָהּ לֹא יִגְרָע
Transliteration:
'Im-'acheret yiqqach-lo, she'erah kesutah ve'onatah lo yigra'.
A close rendering is:
“If he takes another woman for himself, he must not diminish her food, her clothing, or her marital rights.”
The Hebrew word שְׁאֵרָהּ (she'erah) refers here to her food or sustenance.
כְּסוּתָהּ (kesutah) refers to her clothing.
וְעֹנָתָהּ (ve'onatah) is traditionally understood as her conjugal or marital rights, although the precise lexical interpretation has been discussed by scholars.
And then comes the command:
לֹא יִגְרָע (*lo yigra').
“He shall not diminish.”
He shall not reduce.
He shall not deprive her.
Notice what the command actually does.
It does not say, “You should take another wife.”
It does not say, “Multiple wives are My ideal for marriage.”
It does not promise spiritual rewards to men who accumulate wives.
Instead, it places an enforceable obligation upon a man in a society where such arrangements existed.
The woman must not be deprived of what is owed to her.
And the following verse makes the protection even more striking.
Exodus 21:11 declares that if the required provisions are not given, she may go out freely, without payment.
In other words, the law does not merely recognize her vulnerability. It provides a remedy when her rights are violated.
That distinction matters enormously.
A law regulating an existing practice is not necessarily a declaration that the practice represents God's perfect design.
Consider how laws work even today.
A government may establish legal protections for children whose parents divorce without declaring that divorce is the ideal outcome for every marriage.
A law may regulate the treatment of prisoners without declaring that every imprisonment is just.
A law may establish safeguards for people caught in exploitative circumstances without endorsing the circumstances that made those safeguards necessary.
The existence of regulation does not automatically establish moral approval.
But we must be equally careful not to oversimplify.
Exodus 21:10 does genuinely contemplate a man taking another wife. The verse does not explicitly prohibit the practice, and other Old Testament laws also address households with multiple wives.
Deuteronomy 21:15–17, for example, protects the inheritance rights of a firstborn son when a man has two wives, one loved and the other unloved.
That passage does not erase the reality of polygamy in ancient Israel.
It confronts the injustice that can arise within such a household.
And that brings us to an uncomfortable but essential truth.
God's law sometimes restrained the damage caused by human hardness without presenting the damaged arrangement as the original ideal.
How can we know that this distinction is biblical rather than an excuse invented by Christians to escape a difficult passage?
Because Jesus Himself teaches us to read the Law this way.
And what He says changes everything.
In Matthew 19, the Pharisees confront Jesus with a question about divorce.
They appeal to Moses.
Jesus answers by taking them somewhere unexpected.
Not merely to another legal regulation.
Not to the customs of Israel's patriarchs.
Not to the practices of the surrounding nations.
He takes them back to creation.
Jesus says:

“Have ye not read, that he which made them at the beginning made them male and female, And said, For this cause shall a man leave father and mother, and shall cleave to his wife: and they twain shall be one flesh?” — Matthew 19:4–5, KJV
Then He declares:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.” — Matthew 19:6, KJV
The Pharisees respond by asking why Moses permitted divorce.
And Jesus gives one of the most important interpretive statements in the New Testament:
“Moses because of the hardness of your hearts suffered you to put away your wives: but from the beginning it was not so.” — Matthew 19:8, KJV
Read those final words slowly.
But from the beginning it was not so.
Jesus is explicitly addressing divorce, not giving a direct explanation of Exodus 21:10.
We must respect that distinction.
But His reasoning reveals something profound about how we should understand the relationship between the creation ideal and certain Mosaic concessions.
A practice can be addressed or permitted within the Law without representing what God established at creation.
The existence of a Mosaic provision does not, by itself, prove that the provision describes God's highest intention for human relationships.
And when Jesus wants to explain the foundation of marriage, He points to Genesis.
Not to Abraham's household.
Not to Jacob's household.
Not to Solomon's palace.
To the beginning.
Genesis 2:24 says:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.” — KJV
In the Hebrew, the climactic phrase is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד — basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Not merely a business arrangement.
Not a collection of partners assembled for status, pleasure, or political advantage.
A profound union.
The Hebrew word echad means “one.” It does not, by itself, settle every possible question about numerical exclusivity. We should not make a single word carry more weight than the text gives it.
But the creation account presents one man and one woman joined in a covenantal union, and Jesus explicitly appeals to that union as foundational for understanding marriage.
In Matthew 19:5, the Greek phrase is:
σάρκα μίαν — sarka mian.
“One flesh.”
Jesus is not embarrassed by Genesis.
He does not treat creation as an outdated starting point that Israel eventually improved upon.
He brings His listeners back to it.
And the apostle Paul does something equally remarkable in Ephesians 5:31–32.
He quotes Genesis 2:24 and connects the mystery of marriage to Christ and the church.
The picture is not of Christ accumulating competing brides for His own advantage.
It is of Christ loving His church and giving Himself for her.
Marriage, in this Christian understanding, is meant to bear witness to covenantal faithfulness, sacrificial love, and union.
That is a very different picture from a powerful man asking how many women he can legally possess.
But perhaps another objection has already formed in your mind.
“What about Abraham?”
“What about Jacob?”
“What about David?”
“What about Solomon?”
If polygamy was contrary to God's creation design, why did so many significant biblical figures practice it?
And why did God continue working through them?
That question deserves more than a quick religious slogan.
Abraham had Sarah, and through Sarah's initiative he also took Hagar.
But look at what happened.
Genesis 16 records tension, mistreatment, and Hagar's flight into the wilderness.
The household did not become a beautiful demonstration of harmonious marital expansion.
It became a place where a vulnerable woman suffered.
And there, in the wilderness, something extraordinary happened.
God saw her.
Hagar called upon the name of the LORD who spoke to her, saying:
“Thou God seest me.” — Genesis 16:13, KJV
The Hebrew expression associated with her confession is:
אֵל רֳאִי — El Ro'i.
Commonly understood as “God who sees me,” although the precise nuance of the phrase is discussed.
Think about that.
In a story where powerful people made decisions affecting a vulnerable woman's body, future, and security, Scripture pauses to show us that God saw the woman who had been pushed aside.
Not merely the patriarch.
Not merely the promised inheritance.
The woman in the wilderness.
And He heard her affliction.
That does not mean every action of Abraham's household was righteous.
It means God's mercy reached someone wounded by that household's decisions.
Then consider Jacob.
His marriages to Leah and Rachel were entangled with deception, rivalry, favoritism, and profound emotional suffering.
Genesis 29:31 says:
“And when the LORD saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb: but Rachel was barren.” — KJV
The Hebrew term translated “hated” can express being unloved or less loved in a comparative relationship, as the surrounding narrative indicates.
Imagine Leah's pain.
To be married, yet painfully aware that your husband's heart is more deeply attached to someone else.
To be present in the household but feel secondary in the relationship.
To wonder whether you must produce something, achieve something, or prove something just to become worthy of affection.
That is not merely ancient history.
There are people reading this who understand that feeling.
You may never have lived in a polygamous household.
But perhaps you know what it means to be treated as an option.
To receive attention only when someone else is unavailable.
To keep giving your heart to someone who keeps reminding you, through words or silence, that you are not their priority.
And perhaps you have quietly wondered whether God sees the humiliation you have learned to hide.
He does.
The God who saw Hagar also saw Leah.
But the Bible's willingness to tell these stories does not mean it endorses every decision made by the people within them.
Biblical description is not automatically biblical prescription.
Scripture tells us that David committed adultery and arranged a man's death.
That does not make adultery or murder acceptable.
Scripture tells us that Abraham sometimes acted from fear.
That does not make dishonesty a virtue.
Scripture tells us that Solomon accumulated wives.
That does not make his household a model for Christian marriage.
In fact, Solomon's story offers one of the clearest warnings.
First Kings 11:3 records that Solomon had seven hundred wives who were princesses and three hundred concubines.
Then the text says his wives turned away his heart.
The tragedy is not hidden.
The man famous for wisdom became a warning about divided allegiance.
Long before Solomon, Deuteronomy 17:17 had warned Israel's future king:
“Neither shall he multiply wives to himself, that his heart turn not away.” — KJV
This command specifically addresses kings. It is not phrased as a universal statutory prohibition of every polygamous marriage in Israel.
That distinction matters.
Nevertheless, it unmistakably rejects the royal accumulation of wives and identifies the spiritual danger involved.
The Old Testament therefore presents a more complex picture than either side of the argument sometimes admits.
It contains polygamous households.
It regulates certain consequences of polygamy.
It does not issue a blanket prohibition of every such household in the Mosaic Law.

Yet its creation narrative presents a foundational one-flesh union, its stories repeatedly reveal the suffering associated with divided households, and its warnings expose the dangers of multiplying wives.
Then the New Testament brings the creation pattern into sharper focus through Jesus' teaching and the apostles' instructions.
First Timothy 3:2 describes an overseer as:
“The husband of one wife.” — KJV
The Greek expression is:
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα — mias gynaikos andra.
Literally, “a one-woman man” or “husband of one wife.”
Scholars discuss whether the expression primarily emphasizes marital faithfulness, monogamy, or both. The phrase should not be made to answer every marital question by itself.
Yet it clearly emphasizes the character of a man whose intimate commitments are marked by fidelity rather than divided or exploitative desire.
And in 1 Corinthians 7:2, Paul writes:
The reciprocal language is significant.
Paul speaks of husband and wife in terms of mutual belonging and responsibility.
He does not portray marriage as an arrangement in which men collect privileges while women merely endure obligations.
Indeed, in 1 Corinthians 7:3–4, Paul emphasizes mutual marital responsibilities in a manner that challenged many assumptions of the ancient world.
The husband has obligations to his wife.
And the wife is not the only person whose body and conduct are accountable within the marriage.
This is not permission for coercion. Christian marital intimacy must be understood through love, dignity, and care, never through the justification of abuse.
Now return to Exodus 21:10.
Do you see what is happening?
The question we began with was:
“Why would God tell a man how to treat multiple wives if polygamy was not His ideal?”
But the passage itself is not primarily asking how much marital privilege a man may claim.
It is demanding that a vulnerable woman not be deprived of what she is owed.
The law is addressing responsibility.
It is restraining injustice within a social arrangement that existed in ancient Israel.
And if those obligations are violated, Exodus 21:11 provides for her release.
This is not a command to pursue polygamy.
Nor is it proof that every polygamous arrangement in ancient Israel was explicitly condemned by that particular law.
It is a legal protection that must be understood within the larger movement of Scripture.
That larger movement leads us to Jesus.
And this is where the discussion stops being merely about an ancient marriage regulation.
Because every one of us knows something about the distance between God's good design and the world we have actually made.
Some of us have experienced that distance through betrayal.
Some through abandonment.
Some through sexual sin.
Some through broken vows.
Some through relationships where one person had all the power and the other was expected to remain silent.
Some through the terrible experience of having Scripture quoted at us by someone who was unwilling to obey its demands of justice, mercy, and love.
And some of us must admit something even harder.
We have been the ones who caused the wound.
We have wanted God's forgiveness while refusing to acknowledge another person's suffering.
We have looked for biblical loopholes instead of biblical holiness.
We have asked, “How much can I get away with?”
When the better question was, “How can my life reflect the character of Jesus Christ?”
That is a dangerous question.
Not because it threatens our salvation through some impossible demand for perfection.
But because it threatens the excuses we have carefully constructed around our favorite sins.
The human heart is extraordinarily skilled at using permission as a substitute for obedience.
We can take a verse written to protect someone vulnerable and twist it into an argument for expanding our own privileges.
We can quote a regulation while ignoring the God who gave it.
We can defend a religious position while becoming cruel to the very people Scripture commands us to love.
And we can win an argument about the Bible while refusing to surrender to the Lord of the Bible.
Jesus warned about this kind of religious blindness.
In John 5:39–40, He confronted people who searched the Scriptures yet refused to come to Him for life.
The tragedy was not that they studied the text too carefully.
It was that their study did not lead them to the One to whom the Scriptures bore witness.
So here is the question that should unsettle us more than the existence of polygamy in ancient Israel.
Are we reading Scripture to become more like Christ—or merely to find support for what we already want?
Because the Gospel does not invite us to become experts at defending our desires.
It calls us to repentance.
And repentance is more than feeling guilty.
The Greek word μετάνοια — metanoia refers to repentance, a change of mind and direction that involves turning toward God.
It is not a magic word that instantly repairs every consequence of sin.
It is not a performance designed to make wounded people trust us again.
It is a genuine turning from sin toward the mercy and lordship of God.
And the beauty of the Gospel is that Jesus does not demand that sinners repair themselves before they may come to Him.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.” — KJV
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we had constructed a respectable reputation.
Not after we had hidden every shameful chapter.
Not after we had learned enough theology to silence every difficult question.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
But His grace does not exist to make us comfortable remaining enslaved to the very sins from which He came to redeem us.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains believers to deny ungodliness and worldly desires and to live in a godly manner.
Grace forgives.
Grace also transforms.
And the cross reveals the difference between the way fallen humanity often exercises power and the way Jesus exercises His.
Human beings frequently use power to take.
Jesus used His power in self-giving love.
Human beings protect their own interests at another person's expense.
Jesus gave Himself for sinners.
Human beings often ask who can be sacrificed to preserve their comfort.
Jesus became the sacrifice that sinners could never provide for themselves.
Ephesians 5:25 commands:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — KJV
That is the measure.
Not how many people a man can claim.
Not how much authority he can exercise.
Not how many ancient precedents he can collect.
But whether his love reflects the sacrificial faithfulness of Christ.
And that command is not a license for anyone to demand that a spouse remain in danger or endure abuse. The love of Christ never gives an abuser divine permission to harm another person.
A Christian understanding of marriage must take seriously both covenantal faithfulness and the protection of human dignity.
Now imagine something.
Imagine Hagar hearing that God sees her.
Imagine Leah discovering that her pain has not escaped heaven's attention.
Imagine the vulnerable woman in Exodus 21 learning that the law does not allow her provision to be casually stripped away when another woman enters the household.
Then imagine Jesus standing before a crowd of broken people.
People with complicated histories.
People with shameful decisions.
People who have been betrayed.
People who have betrayed others.
People whose family stories are too painful to explain in a short testimony.
And imagine Him announcing that the kingdom of God is at hand, calling sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is where the story is moving.
Not toward the celebration of human power.
Toward the reign of God.
Not toward the normalization of injustice.
Toward the One who will judge evil and redeem sinners.
Not toward the idea that every ancient practice must become a modern Christian ideal.
Toward Jesus Christ, who brings the Scriptures into their proper focus.
And perhaps this is the moment when the question becomes personal.
Because there may be someone reading this who has spent years feeling like the second choice.
You have smiled in public while privately grieving the way someone treated you.
You have been told to be patient when what you needed was justice.
You have been told to forgive when the person who wounded you had not even admitted what they did.
You have wondered whether God values the institution more than the human being suffering inside it.
Hear this carefully.
God's concern for covenant faithfulness does not cancel His concern for the vulnerable.
His call to forgiveness does not erase the need for repentance, accountability, or protection.
And His mercy toward sinners does not mean He is indifferent to the people their sins have harmed.
The God revealed in Scripture is not blind to suffering.

The same Bible that records ancient patriarchs and kings also records the tears of Hagar, the anguish of Leah, the cries of the oppressed, and the warnings of prophets against those who abuse their power.
And at the center of the Christian faith stands a crucified Savior.
Jesus Christ.
The One who was despised and rejected.
The One who bore our sins.
The One who rose again.
The One through whom forgiveness and new life are offered to everyone who turns to Him in faith.
That does not mean every broken marriage will be restored.
It does not mean every person who harmed you will repent.
It does not mean every consequence of sin will disappear.
But it does mean your story does not have to end with the worst thing that happened to you—or the worst thing you have done.
In Christ, shame need not have the final word.
Sin need not remain your master.
And the wounds of this fallen world do not possess authority greater than the risen Lord.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by erasing truth.
But by bringing sinners to repentance, offering forgiveness through His blood, and making new life possible through His resurrection.
So, does Exodus 21:10 prove that God approved polygamy as His ideal for marriage?
No.
It proves that the Mosaic Law regulated an existing marital arrangement and required that a vulnerable woman's rights not be diminished.
Does that mean the Old Testament contains no difficult questions about polygamy?
No.
The text is more complex than that, and faithful Christians should be willing to acknowledge its complexity.
Does Jesus give us a foundation for understanding marriage that reaches beyond those ancient arrangements?
Yes.
He takes us back to creation.
And the New Testament develops a vision of marital faithfulness shaped by the covenantal, self-giving love of Christ.
The answer is not to tear Exodus 21:10 out of the Bible.
It is to read it in its context, recognize the protection it establishes, distinguish legal regulation from creation design, and interpret marriage in light of the teaching of Jesus and His apostles.
The God of Exodus is not embarrassed by the difficult circumstances of fallen humanity.
He speaks into them.
He restrains injustice.
He holds people accountable.
And in the fullness of His redemptive work, He directs us to His Son.
But there is one final question I want to leave with you.
Not about Abraham.
Not about Jacob.
Not even about the man in Exodus 21 who takes another wife.
About you.
When Scripture confronts something you would rather defend, will you allow Jesus to correct you?
When the Word exposes a wound you have hidden, will you bring it into His light?
When the Gospel calls you to surrender something you have justified for years, will you trust the Savior enough to obey?
You do not have to manufacture a perfect answer to every difficult Bible passage before you can trust Christ.
But you must not use the difficulty of a passage as an excuse to ignore the Christ who calls you to Himself.
Perhaps today your prayer is simply:

“Lord Jesus, I don't understand everything. But I want to know You. Forgive my sins. Correct what I have misunderstood. Heal what has been wounded. Teach me to love what You love, reject what You reject, and follow You even when Your Word challenges me.”
That is not a weak prayer.
That is the beginning of surrender.
Or tell us honestly: Before reading this, did you believe Exodus 21:10 was God's endorsement of polygamy? Has your understanding changed?
Your question may be the very question another believer has been afraid to ask.
Your testimony may encourage someone who has nearly abandoned the faith because they encountered a difficult passage and thought there was no faithful answer.

And if you need prayer because your own story includes betrayal, abandonment, or spiritual confusion, you can simply comment, “Pray for me.” You do not have to explain what you are not ready to share.
There are people who need more than another argument on social media.
They need Scripture handled carefully.
They need truth without cruelty.
They need compassion without compromise.
They need to discover that Christianity is not built on pretending hard questions do not exist.
It is built upon the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
That is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not to turn the Bible into a collection of sensational arguments.
Not to build a following around fear.
But to help people encounter the Word of God, wrestle honestly with difficult questions, understand the Gospel, and grow in genuine discipleship.
And if you believe this mission is worth sustaining, I want to invite you into something more.
If you have been looking for a way to support Christian teaching that points people back to Jesus, this is one meaningful opportunity.
Those products can be everyday reminders of the truth we are trying to proclaim, but the heart of the mission will always be greater than merchandise.
It is about Christ.
It is about His Word.
It is about people who are tired of shallow answers and hungry for truth.
It is about helping a wounded believer discover that God has not stopped seeing them.
It is about helping a confused reader understand the Scriptures without distorting them.
It is about helping someone who has wandered far from the Lord hear the Gospel again.
And it is about making resources available to people who may never be able to pay for them.
You may never know who reads what you share.
You may never know which person silently returns to the Bible because you refused to mock their question.
You may never know whose view of God changes because someone finally explained a difficult passage without hiding the truth.
But you can be faithful with what is in your hands.
And above all, you can point them to Jesus.
Because the deepest lesson of Exodus 21:10 is not that powerful men should search the Law for permission to take more.
It is that even in a fallen society, God did not allow the vulnerable woman in that law to be treated as though her needs no longer mattered.
And when Jesus came, He revealed the depth of divine love through a sacrifice that no human marriage, ancient or modern, could ever equal.
He did not come to justify our selfishness.
He came to save us from our sins.
He did not come merely to improve our arguments.
He came to reconcile us to God.
He did not come to teach us how to protect our darkness.
He came as the Light of the world.
So the next time someone asks you, “If God opposes polygamy, why did Exodus 21:10 tell men how to treat multiple wives?” don't run from the question.
Open the Bible.
Read the context.
Tell the truth about the ancient world.
Explain the distinction between regulation and divine ideal.
Listen to Jesus.
And remember the woman whose rights the passage was written to protect.
Because sometimes the most revealing thing about a difficult Bible passage is not what it permits powerful people to do.
It is what it refuses to let them take away from someone who has almost nothing.
The world may remember the man who took another wife. But God made sure His Law also spoke about the woman who must not be forgotten.
